attribution_limitations: ECG lead extent of the first-episode ST elevation is stated three ways: anteroseptal leads V1-V4 in the case text, V1-V6 in the Figure 1 caption and Table 1, and "anterolateral leads" in the abstract. The text sentence cites Figure 1. Lead extent is not recorded as fact; do not choose one.

Regional wall-motion pattern on the left ventriculogram is stated differently: apical and mid LV hypokinesis in the abstract versus preserved apical contractility with mid-ventricular akinesia in the Figure 2 caption. The text calls it a mid ventricular variant. Do not choose one pattern.

Cause of the first myasthenia crisis is hedged by the neurology team (probably secondary to Grave's disease and methimazole) and by the authors (might have triggered); no cause is asserted. For the second crisis the authors found no significant trigger.

Figure 4 ("ECG 3 days later") has no stated anchor. The text cites it for resolution of "ST elevations" in the second-episode sentence, whereas the second-episode ECG is described with T wave inversions and ST elevation is described only for the first episode. Which episode and which earlier ECG it follows is unresolved.

Chest pain onset is described as occurring on waking at the LTAC; the first-episode time points (initial ECG, catheterization, TTE) have no calendar or relative times, and "repeat TTE 3 weeks later" has no stated anchor, so only the order words quoted in the relations are recorded.

Pre-admission drug lines (IVIG, prednisone, pyridostigmine, methimazole) are stated as ongoing therapy without a time point, so their action is unknown rather than current. Methimazole is described both as an existing 10 mg daily therapy and as started about three weeks before the first episode.

The discussion sentence on improvement with prolonged hospitalization names neither the patient nor the episode; the next sentences contrast the quicker second-episode resolution, but the sentence itself is unlabelled.
